output.headline: England crush All Blacks for record win, with Lewis Moody joining the haka
output.standfirst:
• England beat New Zealand 37-12, their heaviest-ever defeat to a northern hemisphere side

  • Former captain Lewis Moody, who has motor neurone disease, joined the haka
output.bodyHtml:
Every year the All Blacks come to south-west London it feels like an acid test. And rarely, if ever, have England responded with such class and conviction on this famous old stretch of grass. New Zealand simply could not live with their clear-eyed, motivated opponents who, at times, made their illustrious visitors look horribly second-rate.

If Kiwi fans thought last week’s loss to Wales was painful this was arguably as bad in terms of the reputational damage. The home side were 19-0 up after 36 minutes and had the game all but wrapped up within a couple of minutes of the restart when Ollie Chessum smashed his way over to claim his side’s fourth try. In terms of England’s margin of victory, this was New Zealand’s heaviest loss to any northern hemisphere nation in their proud history.

Related: England hail ‘inspirational’ Moody after thrashing New Zealand

There were even occasions when the fabled silver fern was in danger of being utterly trampled, with almost three-quarters of the game taking place in the New Zealand half. If anything it was England who more closely resembled the slick All Black sides of yesteryear, particularly in the first half when tries from Henry Slade, Jack van Poortvliet and Ben Earl rewarded the hosts’ purposeful approach play, set-piece accuracy and seemingly greater desire.

The significant improvement in their backline fluency is certainly a tribute to, among others, their attack coach, Lee Blackett, but, best of all, England are finally emerging as the all-court team they aspire to be. Their captain, Maro Itoje, had teed this up as “a massive game” in terms of “showing the world where we believe this team can go” and that lofty objective was gloriously achieved despite the pre-game injury withdrawal of the winger Tommy Freeman.

Related: England’s strength in depth finally comes together in landmark All Blacks victory | Andy Bull

The bench also left an impression, as did the sight of England’s former captain Lewis Moody lining up with the current players as they faced the haka. Initially Moody, now an inspiring campaigner for motor neurone research, stood up front before the England team moved in front of him and, in some cases, even entered into the All Black half. As a symbol of intent it was also as powerful as any seen on this ground down the years.

The huge emotional impact, however, had to be balanced against the loss of Freeman with a thigh problem, less than ideal with their other prolific wing, Manny Feyi-Waboso, already sidelined. Cadan Murley stepped up to start on the left wing with Will Joseph switching to the right but England’s sense of purpose was never remotely diluted. As early as the fifth minute they had their first try on the board after Fin Smith spotted some space in behind and Slade was quickest to react to his fly-half’s perfectly weighted grubber kick.

Itoje and his head coach, Steve Borthwick, had both been urging their team to make a fast start and their instructions had clearly not fallen on deaf ears. New Zealand also fell foul of the Australian referee Nic Berry at the breakdown from an early stage and fumbled their lines even when they did make it into the home 22.

England, by contrast, forced their way into the All Black 22 five times inside the first 25 minutes. New Zealand, though, appeared to have picked up one or two lessons from Wales’s heroic goalline stand in Cardiff and initially repeatedly kept them out, most notably when Alex Coles was held up. There was another frustrating false start when Smith kicked the ball dead from a scrum penalty that should have put New Zealand right back into coffin corner.

Could England be in danger of blowing all their good work? Happily for their supporters the answer was to be a resounding “no”. With the All Blacks again under siege close to their own line after another lovely attack by Slade, the slight figure of Van Poortvliet swallow-dived over to score his side’s second try. Then came the defining moment of the half. Earl is an excellent athlete but to watch him blast through the lone tackle of Cam Roigard and storm to the line would have been painful viewing for Tonbridge under-11s, never mind New Zealand.

Ethan de Groot did grab a try back two minutes before the interval but the half-time horror for Kiwis watching aghast through their fingers back at home was about to get even worse. England once again made yards down the middle before moving the ball wide and, not for the first time, there was Chessum to hammer home the final nail in the left corner.

Related: Fading Beauden Barrett a symbol of rabble All Blacks’ joyless decline | Gerard Meagher

It was certainly no way for Beauden Barrett to celebrate his 150th cap, even if the great man did score a smart trademark try from a nice Roigard offload. Otherwise Dave Rennie, a good rugby man suddenly caught in the headlamps of an onrushing locomotive, had very little to console him as England’s replacements maintained the suffocating pressure.

Maybe England could have even eclipsed the 38 points they scored against these same opponents in 2012 when Manu Tuilagi was running amok. They ultimately had to settle for a 62nd minute try scored by the quietly impressive Seb Atkinson, another player whose stock is now rising rapidly. Finals weekend, for the moment, can wait.
output.progress: Former captain Lewis Moody, now an inspiring campaigner for motor neurone research, lined up with the team to face the haka – a powerful symbol of intent.
